name: Matrixyl

lead: Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, Pal-KTTKS) is a lipid-modified fragment of type I procollagen developed by a cosmetic ingredient supplier for anti-wrinkle products. It appears in many serums and eye creams.
Supporting data are mainly from supplier-sponsored or small studies, so independent evidence of visible improvement is limited.

paras: The peptide is thought to mimic collagen breakdown fragments that signal fibroblasts to make new collagen and other matrix components. The palmitoyl group is added to help it cross the skin barrier.
It is considered low-risk, with rare irritation, and is freely sold as a cosmetic. Effects are modest and benefits depend on formulation and the concentration achieved at the target layer.

lead: Matrixyl is the trade name of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS, called palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 before 2006), a lipid-modified peptide used in anti-wrinkle cosmetics. It was launched in 2000 as a personal-care active by the French ingredient manufacturer Sederma [1]. The peptide consists of the five amino acids lysine-threonine-threonine-lysine-serine joined to a 16-carbon palmitic acid chain, which is meant to help it cross the lipid structures of the skin [1][1].

KTTKS is described as a matrikine, a messenger fragment related to the breakdown of collagen. In cell studies it stimulates extracellular matrix production and expression of type I and III collagen [2]. Wikipedia states that in vitro and in vivo studies of its anti-wrinkle efficacy have been published by Sederma and by independent organizations [1]. A 2026 review of peptides in aesthetic dermatology describes matrikine-like peptides as influencing matrix-related responses in experimental systems and surveys the clinical evidence [3].

Matrixyl appears in serums, creams and eye products, often alongside other peptides. Several of the human studies in the sources reviewed are small or compare it with other cosmetic peptides, and evidence for independent, large-scale visible benefit is limited.

paras: Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 is used in anti-wrinkle creams, serums and eye products intended to reduce the appearance of fine lines. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, says it is typically used at very low concentrations and appears in more than 200 formulations [4]. A DailyMed label for a stretch-mark cream lists palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 among several peptides, with external-use warnings [5].

Combinations are common. The Matrixyl 3000 trade blend contains palmitoyl tripeptide-1 (Pal-GHK) and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 [6]. A 2025 in vitro study examined palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 with another peptide and injectable platelet-rich fibrin on dermal fibroblasts [7].

A 2023 double-blind randomized trial compared an acetylhexapeptide-3 cream with a palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 cream for crow's feet [8]. Grokipedia describes a 12-week double-blind split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55 and a 28-day periocular study with reported reductions in wrinkle depth, but those figures come from an AI-generated summary and are not independently confirmed in the other sources reviewed [4].

A 2004 randomized trial in 20 breast cancer patients compared a cream containing Matrixyl with CM glucan and hydroxyprolisilan C against Bepanthol lotion during radiotherapy and found no differences in median skin toxicity scores between groups, with mild itchiness and sporadic efflorescences more frequent with the cream [9]. This concerns radiation skin care, not wrinkles.

A 2025 review of peptides for skin senescence discusses KTTKS among candidates [10]. Permeation is a recurring theme: a 2026 study characterizes how cosmetic actives, including peptides found in Matrixyl 3000, permeate human stratum corneum [6], and a 2025 study tested nanomicelles to improve transdermal delivery of palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 as a model signal peptide [11].

Wikipedia and reviews describe it as a cosmetic ingredient without notable toxicity concerns; Grokipedia states it is non-sensitizing and non-irritating at reported concentrations [1][4]. In the radiotherapy study, mild itchiness occurred more often with the Matrixyl-containing cream than with the control lotion [9]. A comparison of novel KTTKS analogues examined cytotoxicity on fibroblasts and effects on protease activity [2].

Matrikines are messenger peptides that regulate cell activity through specific receptors and activate genes involved in extracellular matrix renewal and cell proliferation [1]. KTTKS originates from the proteolytic breakdown of collagen, and its palmitoylated form is more stable [2]. Laboratory work shows that C16-KTTKS stimulates collagen production in dermal and corneal fibroblasts in a concentration-dependent manner close to the concentration at which it self-assembles into nanotape structures, suggesting the two are related [12]. Researchers have designed lipopeptide variants carrying cycloalkane chains or carnosine motifs based on the KTTKS sequence [13][14].

Pal-KTTKS is a five-residue lipopeptide whose palmitoyl group is attached through an amide bond to the first lysine [1][4]. Its self-assembly into peptide amphiphile nanostructures has been studied in materials science [12][13].

Sederma (now part of Croda, according to Grokipedia) launched palmitoyl pentapeptide as Matrixyl in 2000, and the INCI name was changed from pentapeptide-3 to pentapeptide-4 in 2006 [1][4]. It is widely cited as a prototype of cosmetic signal peptides; later peptide products such as Matrixyl 3000 expanded the line [6].

Community discussion in the sources reviewed is minimal. A 2013 T Nation poster asked about peptides including TB-500, GHK, Biopeptide EL and Matrixyl in the context of healing times and scarring [15]. No Reddit or looksmax.org threads were reviewed.

Published human studies are few. They include a double-blind randomized comparison of acetylhexapeptide-3 and palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 creams for crow's feet [8] and a 20-patient randomized trial of a Matrixyl-containing cream during breast radiotherapy that found no difference in skin toxicity versus standard lotion [9]. Reviews of aesthetic peptides summarize the clinical evidence and note that much of the mechanistic data are experimental [3][10]. Other research on Matrixyl consists of cell studies, hairless mouse experiments using it as a positive control, and delivery and materials work [7][11][12][13][16].

timeline.event: Sederma launches palmitoyl pentapeptide as Matrixyl [1].
Randomized trial of a Matrixyl-containing cream during breast radiotherapy is published [9].
The INCI name changes from palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 to pentapeptide-4 [1].
